reconcile.connective: Harmonizers read Deuteronomy as condemning the Moabites' hiring and intent, not a curse that ever landed — God turned that design into a blessing.

discrepancy.connective: Steven DiMattei presses the discrepancy on source-critical grounds: the Numbers narrative never shows Balaam wishing to curse Israel, whereas Deuteronomy 23 (with Joshua 24 and Nehemiah 13) presupposes that hostile intent, marking two divergent traditions rather than one account.

skeptic.name: Steven DiMattei
skeptic.work: Contradictions in the Bible, entry #291 "Does Balaam wish to curse Israel or not?"
skeptic.attribution: Steven DiMattei, Contradictions in the Bible (contradictionsinthebible.com), #291

excerpts.excerpt_text: It is true God turned the curse into a blessing (Deu 23:5), not only changing the word in Balaam's mouth, but making that really turn to the honour and advantage of Israel which was designed for their ruin. But though the design was defeated, and overruled for good, the Moabites' wickedness was not the less provoking.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Directly resolves the tension: Deuteronomy's ground for excluding Moab is the attempt/design to curse, which God overruled into a blessing, not a curse that actually took effect. Distinguishes hiring/intent from result.

pd_work.resource: Matthew Henry, Commentary on the Whole Bible (1706-14), on Deuteronomy 23:1-8
pd_work.author: Matthew Henry
pd_work.note: Treats this passage directly: explains that Deuteronomy faults the Moabites' hiring and design to curse, which God turned into a blessing, so no actual curse contradicts the Numbers narrative.

link.title: GotQuestions: What does the Bible say about God turning curses into blessings (Deuteronomy 23:5)?
link.note: Live apologetic treatment of Deut 23:5 and the Balaam episode: Balaam was hired to curse but God turned the curse into a blessing.
